div.head: About the eLiebermann Project
div.p: The eLiebermann database is a digital research platform for the laws and legal language of early England. Its foundation is Felix Liebermann's Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen (1903–16), still the standard complete edition of the early English laws, which it makes searchable, interlinked and accessable to Anglophone readers. Around that core it collates later editions, translations and scholarship, so that the text of a law, the words it uses, and what scholars have said about both can be studied in one place.
The platform has three parts:

list.item: The eLiebermann Lawcodes Database presents the laws clause by clause, according to Liebermann's own editorial divisions. Each clause gives the Old English or Latin text as Liebermann prints it, labelled by manuscript; his German translation, with an English rendering of it; and, where they exist in the public domain, the texts and translations of later editors. Every clause is newly indexed by the offences, people and places it concerns. Similarities and points of comparison between clauses across the corpus made by Liebermann and later scholars are gathered and included as links, with citations.

The eLiebermann Legal Dictionary is a digital edition of Liebermann's Wörterbuch (volume II, part 1), the dictionary of the Old English, Latin and French words of the laws. Every abbreviation, siglum and grammatical term in an entry is linked to its expansion and an English translation, every law it cites is linked to that clause in the Lawcodes Database, and headwords are in the process of being linked to entries in other dictionaries.

The eLiebermann Guide to the Gesetze expands and translates the apparatus of the Gesetze: Liebermann's sigla for the law codes, his list of manuscripts, and his grammatical abbreviations, with his own account of how to read the dictionary.

div.p: The project grows out of research on the language and composition of the earliest English law codes. Its aims are to open Liebermann's foundational work to more scholars, and to facilitate new research into the earliest English written laws.
At present eLiebermann holds:

list.item: 9,246 dictionary entries, the whole of the Wörterbuch;
2,547 clauses from 78 law codes and legal texts, from the laws of Æthelberht of Kent to those of William I and Henry I;
the texts and translations of a number of more modern editions, among them those of F. L. Attenborough and A. J. Robertson;
1,348 cross-references between clauses from Liebermann's apparatus, and about 1,500 more from later scholars, each linked in both directions.

div.p: eLiebermann is a work in progress. New material is added, and existing material corrected, continuously (see Code and data, below).

div.head: Felix Liebermann and Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen
div.p: Felix Liebermann (born Berlin, 20 July 1851; died Berlin, 7 October 1925) was a German historian of medieval England, and the foremost authority of his generation on Anglo-Saxon and Anglo-Norman law. He came from a prosperous Jewish family in Berlin; the painter Max Liebermann was his elder brother. He began in business, in banking and the textile trade, and it was while he was living in Manchester that he became interested in English history. In 1873 he went to Göttingen to study it under Georg Waitz and Reinhold Pauli, and took his doctorate in 1875 with a study of the Dialogus de Scaccario. From 1877 to 1885 he worked as an editor for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica, for which he edited extracts from thirteenth-century English historians.

Liebermann held no regular university post, and spent the rest of his life as an independent scholar in Berlin. In a long series of studies he edited and explained the legal compilations of the early twelfth century through which most of the Old English laws were transmitted: the Quadripartitus (1892), the Consiliatio Cnuti (1893), the Leges Edwardi Confessoris (1896) and the Leges Henrici (1901). The universities of Oxford and Cambridge gave him honorary degrees in 1896. His English lecture The National Assembly in the Anglo-Saxon Period appeared in 1913.
His great work, Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, was published in Halle for the Savigny-Stiftung, in three volumes and four parts:

list.item: I. Text und Übersetzung (1903): the texts of all the laws, from Æthelberht to the Anglo-Norman compilations, with the readings of every manuscript printed in parallel columns, a German translation, and marginal cross-references between clauses;
II.1. Wörterbuch (1906): a dictionary of every word in the laws;
II.2. Rechts- und Sachglossar (1912): a glossary of legal and historical subjects;
III. Einleitung zu jedem Stück; Erklärungen zu einzelnen Stellen (1916): an introduction to each text and a commentary on individual passages.

div.p: More than a century later the Gesetze remains the edition from which the laws are commonly cited, and much of what has been written on early English law since rests on it. But it is not an easy book to use. It is written in a heavily abbreviated academic German, it depends on hundreds of sigla, and its apparatus is dense and occasionally inconsistent. Parts of its scholarship have also been substantially revised by later studies. eLiebermann keeps Liebermann's text as he printed it, and sets beside it the work of the century since.

div.head: How Entries Are Made
div.p: Both the Legal Dictionary and the Lawcodes Database are built from the printed Gesetze, and both add material that Liebermann does not have. The editorial work combines human scholarship with machine-assisted transcription, collation and encoding.
div.head: Transcription and collation
div.p: Every dictionary entry has been transcribed twice, independently. The project team keyed the entries by hand into Word documents, preserving and at times intervening to regularise Liebermann's system of typography. A machine transcription was separately made in 2026 from page images of the Wörterbuch by Claude, a large language model developed by Anthropic. The two transcriptions are then collated and cross-checked entry by entry and word by word. Each disagreement is classified (a slip in one transcription or the other, a difference of typography only, a different division between entries) and, where it cannot be settled from the transcriptions alone, it is checked by the editor against the printed volume. A report of every collation, and a running list of readings still to be checked against the print, are kept in the project's data.

Liebermann's typography encodes meaning in a number of ways: roman type is the language of the laws, italic is Liebermann's German and/or grammatical commentary, bold marks headwords, and a superscript L or F distinguishes a Latin or French word. Transcription recorded page breaks, and every entry is linked to its page in a scan of the printed volume; users of the database can check entries against Liebermann's original printed version.
div.head: Encoding and linking
div.p: Every dictionary entry and every law-code clause is a separate file in TEI XML, the international standard for scholarly digital editions (Text Encoding Initiative, P5). Within an entry, law-code sigla, manuscript sigla and grammatical abbreviations are identified automatically, by longest match against the authority lists created by the editor, and so are linked to their expansions. Each citation of a law is normalised to a standard key that follows the citation style of scholarship (law code and clause number) and resolved to its clause in the Lawcodes Database. Liebermann's own cross-references between entries (s. WORD) become links, and headwords are linked to the Bosworth–Toller Anglo-Saxon Dictionary.

Where a correction is made (e.g. where Liebermann's printed entry sends readers to a headword that does not exist, or to an incorrect spelling) an "Editor's note" is included on the entry page, explaining the change or correction.
div.head: The Lawcodes Database
div.p: The database is compiled in a master spreadsheet of more than fifty fields for each clause, from which the clause files are generated by script. For each clause the spreadsheet records, at least: Liebermann's text of each manuscript he prints, identified by his siglum, with his page and section number; his German translation; and an English rendering of his German. That rendering is a deliberately close, semi-literal translation made with the help of an LLM (Claude, a Large Language Model created by Anthropic, 2026) so that readers can follow what Liebermann understood the law to say. This 'translation' is labelled as such on every clause page; it is a crib to help readers through Liebermann's German, not a new translation of the Old English. The editor has intervened to correct some of its more egregious misprisions, where these have been noticed; for the rest, users are on their own! Caution with these renderings is advised. The texts and translations of modern editions are entered with their page references and have been checked against the printed books. Liebermann's marginal cross-references were transcribed from the page images of volume I, and the cross-references and comparisons of later scholars have been collected from their studies, editions, footnotes and tables of sources; each records its source and page, and each is linked in both directions. These are incomplete, and will continue to be added over time. The subject index of offences, people and places is the project's own editorial work, and does not reflect the subjects and concepts recorded in Liebermann's Vol II.2Rechts- und Sachglossar.

Checking is recorded clause by clause: the foot of each clause page says what has been checked, and against which page of which book. This work is ongoing; individual clauses will record when a final check has been made by a member of the project team.
div.head: Review and publication
div.p: All the project's text and data are kept under version control in a Git repository. Every addition or correction, by a person or by a script, is proposed as a separate, documented change. Errors can be reported, and new entries suggested, through Make a suggestion or the Suggest a change link at the foot of every entry.

div.head: Citing eLiebermann
div.p: When you use eLiebermann, you can use the linked archive.org pdfs of Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen to confirm the text and cite directly to Liebermann:
Felix Liebermann, ed. and trans., Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, 3 vols (Halle: Niemeyer, 1903–16).
If you would like to cite directly to the eLiebermann database, you can use this form:

A dictionary entry: “bocland”, eLiebermann Legal Dictionary, ed. Anya Adair, https://notamitchell.github.io/law/entry.html?id=bocland (accessed 15 October 2026); after Felix Liebermann, ed. and trans., Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, 3 vols (Halle: Niemeyer, 1903–16), II.1, p. 26.

A law-code clause: “Ine 23.2”, eLiebermann Lawcodes Database, ed. Anya Adair, https://notamitchell.github.io/law/law.html?id=Ine_23-2 (accessed 15 October 2026); after Felix Liebermann, ed. and trans., Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen, 3 vols (Halle: Niemeyer, 1903–16), I, p. 98.
When quoting a modern edition or translation from a clause page, please cite that edition as well; its full reference is given on the page.

div.head: Funding
div.p: The work described here was supported by a grant from the Research Grants Council of Hong Kong (General Research Fund, Project No. HKU 17604022), for the project The Language and Style of the Earliest English Law Codes (PI: Anya Adair).

div.head: Code and data
div.p: The site's code and all its data are on GitHub at github.com/notamitchell/law: the dictionary entries and clauses as TEI XML, the authority lists of law codes, manuscripts and abbreviations, the scripts that build the site, and the reports of collation and checking.
Liebermann's text and translation are in the public domain.
